stem: A private company lessee cannot readily determine the rate implicit in its new warehouse lease and has made no risk-free rate election. What discount rate does it use?

choices.text: Its incremental borrowing rate — the default when the implicit rate is not readily determinable
A risk-free rate — it applies automatically to private companies
An estimate of the rate implicit in the lease
Any reasonable rate, as an accounting policy choice

feedback: The hierarchy in 842-20-30-3 runs: implicit rate whenever readily determinable, otherwise the incremental borrowing rate — and the risk-free rate only ever replaces the incremental borrowing rate by election, which this lessee has not made. Answer (b) turns an election into a default; (c) misreads 'readily determinable' as 'estimable' — a rate that must be estimated is not readily determinable and is not used; (d) mistakes a measurement hierarchy for a free policy choice. Re-study block 2 (S-02, the three sentences).

stem: A lessee has made the risk-free rate election for its vehicle class and signs a four-year vehicle lease. Which rate does it use to discount the payments?

choices.text: A risk-free rate for a period comparable with four years — for example, a four-year Treasury yield
The overnight federal funds rate, since it is the purest risk-free rate
Its incremental borrowing rate — the election only applies to real estate
The ten-year Treasury yield, as the standard benchmark rate

feedback: The paragraph requires the risk-free rate to be determined 'using a period comparable with that of the lease term' — a four-year lease takes a rate for a comparable four-year period. Answers (b) and (d) both drop the comparable-period discipline, reaching for a rate because it is low or because it is famous; (c) invents a real-estate restriction — the election attaches to whichever classes the lessee elects, and this lessee elected vehicles. Re-study block 3 (S-03, what the rate is).
_source: sources/asc842/842-20-30-3.txt ('a period comparable with that of the lease term'); sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt BC22 (Treasury rates as the operable example)

stem: Before ASU 2021-09, what made many private company lessees reluctant to use the risk-free rate election?

choices.text: It was all-or-nothing: electing meant using the low risk-free rate for every lease, inflating the liabilities that mattered most
Risk-free rates were not publicly available for most lease terms
The election required disclosure that most companies found too burdensome
The FASB prohibited applying it to real estate leases

feedback: The original election applied entity-wide, to all leases — and because a risk-free rate is lower than a real borrowing rate, electing meant recognizing larger liabilities and right-of-use assets everywhere, real estate included. That is exactly the reluctance the Board recorded, and why ASU 2021-09 remade the election by class. Answer (b) has it backwards — public availability at many maturities is the rate's chief virtue; (c) reverses history — the class disclosure arrived with the amendment, it did not precede it; (d) invents a prohibition where there was only an unattractive all-or-nothing choice. Re-study block 4 (S-04, the history).
_source: sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt BC6, BC8–BC9, BC15 (all-or-nothing reluctance and the by-class fix)

stem: Compared with discounting the same lease payments at its 7% incremental borrowing rate, a lessee that discounts them at a 4% risk-free rate will initially report:

choices.text: A larger lease liability and a larger right-of-use asset
A smaller lease liability, because the rate is lower
The same amounts — the discount rate does not affect measurement
A larger lease liability but a smaller right-of-use asset

feedback: A lower rate removes less of the payments in discounting, so the present value — and therefore both the lease liability and the matching right-of-use asset — starts larger. Answer (b) is the common inversion: a lower rate means less discounting, not less liability; (c) forgets that the liability is a present value, which is exactly what the rate drives; (d) breaks the initial symmetry between the liability and the asset. Re-study block 5 (S-05, the worked trade).
_source: sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt BC8 (lower rate → greater liabilities and ROU assets); the 7%/4% figures are illustrative arithmetic — see drafts/ASC842-PCX-02-review.md

stem: Which of the following lessees is prohibited from making the risk-free rate election in 842-20-30-3?

choices.text: A public business entity
A not-for-profit entity that is a conduit bond obligor
An employee benefit plan that files financial statements with the SEC
A private company with an easily determined incremental borrowing rate

feedback: The paragraph draws one line: the election is available to a lessee that is not a public business entity. Not-for-profit entities — conduit bond obligors included — and employee benefit plans are not public business entities, so (b) and (c) may elect; the Board said so expressly in ASU 2021-09. If (b) or (c) tempted you, you are likely thinking of the common control expedient in lesson 4, which does exclude them — the two scopes differ. And (d) confuses convenience with eligibility: nothing requires a lessee to struggle before electing. Re-study block 7 (S-07, who gets it).
_source: sources/asc842/842-20-30-3.txt ('not a public business entity'); sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt Summary and BC13 (NFPs including conduit bond obligors, and EBPs, are in scope)

stem: A lessee that is not a public business entity has elected the risk-free rate for its equipment class. For one equipment lease, the rate implicit in the lease is readily determinable. What rate applies to that lease?

choices.text: The rate implicit in the lease — it applies whenever readily determinable, election or not
The risk-free rate — the election covers every lease in the class
The lessee's incremental borrowing rate
The lower of the implicit rate and the risk-free rate

feedback: The paragraph's first sentence — use the implicit rate whenever it is readily determinable — keeps applying inside an elected class; ASU 2021-09 added that requirement precisely because practice was unsure, and the Board's Basis for Conclusions works this exact equipment-class example. Answer (b) reads the election as sealing off the class, the interpretation the Board rejected; (c) skips both the implicit rate and the election to land on the default neither applies here; (d) invents a lower-of test the standard does not contain. Re-study block 6 (S-06, the exception inside the election).
_source: sources/asc842/842-20-30-3.txt (first sentence); sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt BC17–BC19 (the equipment-class example)

stem: How does an eligible lessee make the risk-free rate election, and for what period is the rate determined?

choices.text: As an accounting policy election by class of underlying asset, using a rate for a period comparable with the lease term
Entity-wide for all leases, using the shortest available Treasury rate
Lease by lease, using a rate for a period comparable with the lease term
By class of underlying asset, always using the ten-year Treasury rate

feedback: Both mechanics come from the paragraph's final sentence: an accounting policy election made by class of underlying asset, with the rate determined using a period comparable with that of the lease term. Answer (b) is the pre-2021-09 entity-wide rule the Board replaced, with a rate-shopping error added; (c) trades the by-class policy for lease-by-lease cherry-picking, which a policy election exists to prevent; (d) gets the class right but freezes the rate at one maturity, breaking the comparable-period requirement. Re-study blocks 2 and 3 (S-02 and S-03).

stem: Which statement describes what ASU 2021-09 changed about the risk-free rate election?

choices.text: It allowed the election by class of underlying asset instead of entity-wide, and required the implicit rate whenever readily determinable
It created the risk-free rate election for the first time
It replaced the risk-free rate with a corporate bond rate
It extended the election to public business entities

feedback: The amendment took an existing all-or-nothing election and made it by class, added the disclosure of elected classes, and settled the open question in favor of the implicit rate whenever it is readily determinable. Answer (b) misdates the election — Topic 842 has had it since 2016; ASU 2021-09 reshaped it; (c) is the alternative the Board considered and rejected because corporate bond rates are not publicly published by a reliable source; (d) reverses the scope — the election remains closed to public business entities. Re-study block 4 (S-04, the history).
_source: sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt Summary (main provisions), BC6 (2016 origin), BC21–BC23 (corporate bond rate rejected)

stem: A lessee is weighing its estimated 7% incremental borrowing rate against a 4% risk-free rate for a new five-year operating lease. Which of the following is a consequence of electing the risk-free rate?

choices.text: A larger initial lease liability and right-of-use asset, in exchange for skipping the work of determining an incremental borrowing rate
Higher total lease expense over the lease term
A smaller lease liability, since less interest accrues at a lower rate
No effect on the financial statements — only the discounting mechanics change

feedback: The election trades measurement for effort: discounting at a lower rate leaves a larger present value on both sides of the balance sheet, and in return the lessee never has to build or defend an incremental borrowing rate. For an operating lease, total expense over the term is the sum of the payments either way, so (b) fails; (c) is the interest-intuition inversion — a lower rate discounts less, it does not owe less; (d) understates a change that moves both the liability and the asset. Re-study block 5 (S-05, the trade in dollars).
_source: sources/asc842/ASU_2021-09.txt BC7 (the avoided IBR cost), BC8 (greater liabilities and ROU assets); figures are illustrative arithmetic — see drafts/ASC842-PCX-02-review.md
